posts.title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
posts.summary: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.”  Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on…
bullets: Nvidia privately informed Representative Bill Foster that implementing geotracking for advanced AI chips is technically feasible, contradicting the Semiconductor Industry Association's public claims that such mandates are infeasible.

The proposed Chip Security Act aims to mandate location verification for high-end AI hardware to prevent illegal exports to China, a measure currently under consideration for the National Defense Authorization Act.
Nvidia's 'Fleet Intelligence' tool, launched in December 2025, already demonstrates the company's capability to monitor chip performance and location across global data centers.
The legislative push for stricter chip oversight has gained significant momentum following the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang and allegations of his involvement with a foreign intelligence asset.

posts.title: Designing Edge AI SoCs At Near-Threshold: Why Foundation IP Can Help You Break Down The Power Wall
posts.summary:
Traditional voltage scaling is no longer sufficient to deliver real-time performance within tight energy and thermal limits.
The post Designing Edge AI SoCs At Near-Threshold: Why Foundation IP Can Help You Break Down The Power Wall appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Traditional voltage scaling is no longer sufficient to deliver real-time performance within tight energy and thermal limits.
Lowering operating voltage is a key to SoC power optimization.
In advanced FinFET processes at ~0.4–0.5V, it can also start to become a design risk.
As edge AI pushes inference closer to endpoints, edge-AI SoCs must deliver real-time performance within tight energy and thermal limits.
Traditional voltage scaling is no longer sufficient.

posts.title: The Memory Challenge Of Physical AI
posts.summary:
Right-size the memory hierarchy around the device's data streams, reuse patterns, latency requirements, and operating constraints.
The post The Memory Challenge Of Physical AI appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Right-size the memory hierarchy around the device’s data streams, reuse patterns, latency requirements, and operating constraints.
Most AI hardware conversations start with compute, which is understandable since accelerators are visible, easy to compare, and often tied to headline performance metrics.
Physical AI broadens that conversation by placing greater emphasis on how compute, memory, and data movement work together under real-world operating constraints.
For intelligent systems that must see, interpret, decide, and act in the physical world in real time, it’s critical that the right data reaches the right engine at the right time.
As a result, data movement has become an increasingly important consideration when architecting physical AI systems.
